property_summary: For every call, the reference contract's owner() returns the address that was set during construction/ownership transfer (initially the deployer), whereas the mutant always returns address(0) so there exists some caller for which the returned owner address differs (the rule: owner() == deployer address), which the mutant violates.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract reverts if newOwner == address(0) (so it never sets owner to zero), whereas the mutant allows setting owner to address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner (the zero address) and thus changes owner() to address(0).

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never results in owner() being set to the zero address in the correct contract; the mutant allows setting owner() to address(0) when newOwner == address(0), violating this invariant.

For any caller, after transferOwnership(newOwner) is called by the current owner, the reference contract never sets owner() to address(0); the mutant allows owner() == address(0) when newOwner == address(0), so the property is violated for that input.

For every caller who is the current owner and every newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract either reverts when newOwner == address(0) or results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant violates this by allowing owner() to become address(0) when newOwner == address(0) (i.e. the invariant "owner() != address(0) after a successful transferOwnership call" holds for the reference but is broken by the mutant for some inputs).

For every caller who is the current owner and every non-eoa newOwner address (i.e. an address with contract code), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract always results in owner() equal to newOwner (and never sets owner() to address(0)); the mutant can set owner() to address(0) when the owner forwards a call from a contract that triggers transferOwnership with newOwner == address(0) (the difference is that the reference reverts for zero newOwner while mutant accepts it).

After calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the OwnershipTransferred event emitted by the contract must report (previousOwner, newOwner) where previousOwner equals owner() before the call and newOwner equals owner() after the call; the mutant emits the event before updating storage so observers seeing owner() during the event will observe swapped/incorrect pairing for some inputs.

Invariant: after transferOwnership(newOwner) returns, the OwnershipTransferred event reports previousOwner equal to owner() before the call and newOwner equal to owner() after the call; the mutant emits the event before updating storage, causing the pair in the event to be (oldOwner, oldOwner) when newOwner equals oldOwner or swapped for some inputs (detectable by comparing event arguments to storage before/after).

For any caller A and any newOwner X (non-zero, possibly equal to A), after calling transferOwnership(X) from the current owner A, the contract's owner() becomes X (the state is updated) — the mutant emits OwnershipTransferred before updating storage which can cause the observable owner() during the emitted event to mismatch and in some cases lead to different observable behavior when an event listener (implemented as a contract called as part of transfer) queries owner() during the event emission; we detect this by having an adversarial recipient that, when transferOwnership attempts to emit the event, executes a callback that reads owner() and causes a detectable difference in stored reentrancy/state-observation between reference and mutant.

When the owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the OwnershipTransferred event must be emitted reporting the previous owner equal to the owner() value before the call and the new owner equal to owner() after the call — this requires the storage _owner be updated before any external observation during event emission; the mutant emits the event before updating _owner, which allows an adversarial contract invoked during event emission to observe a different owner() and thus break this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero newOwner, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the OwnershipTransferred emission observed during the call must see previousOwner equal to the pre-call owner and newOwner equal to the post-call owner; the mutant emits the event before updating storage allowing an adversarial contract invoked during event emission to observe a different owner and thus violate this rule for some inputs.

Invariant: transferOwnership must only succeed when msg.sender == owner (or caller is owner) — the reference rejects calls when owner is zero, but the mutant incorrectly allows anyone to call transferOwnership when owner == address(0), so there exists an input (a caller address) that makes mutant succeed while reference reverts.
Only the contract owner can change rewardDistributor (setRewardDistributor) — i.e., calling setRewardDistributor by msg.sender that is not owner always reverts.
Only the current owner can successfully call setRewardDistributor (calls from non-owner revert).
Only calls to setRewardDistributor made by the contract owner may succeed (non-owner callers revert).

setRewardDistributor succeeds when and only when msg.sender is the contract owner in the original contract, so any caller who is not the owner will have the call revert (i.e., non-owner calls always revert).
In the original contract, setRewardDistributor succeeds iff msg.sender is the owner; therefore for any caller who is the owner the call must not revert.
